data: © NASA — Artemis II mission, April 2026. First crewed flight beyond LEO since Apollo 17 (1972). Hybrid free-return lunar flyby — Orion swung around the Moon's far side at ~6,545 km altitude and returned to Earth without lunar orbit insertion. The mission that inspired Orrery.
NASA Artemis II post-flight report; ICPS raised the perigee; Orion's own service-module engine performed TLI on flight day 2
NASA Artemis II flight reconstruction: outbound + return TCMs executed
NASA Artemis II free-return flyby (2026-04-06): no lunar orbit insertion burn; closest approach ~6,545 km (4,067 mi) above the far side; maximum distance 406,771 km, the human record

NASA Artemis II: ICPS raised perigee and apogee into a high Earth orbit; Orion's service-module engine made the ~0.39 km/s TLI ~25 h after launch; total derived from the 350 km parking orbit to C3 -1.7 km2/s2 (cislunar_profile): sqrt(C3 + 2mu/r) - sqrt(mu/r) = 3.1 km/s, split between the ICPS raises and Orion's TLI; free return needs no LOI or TEI burn (Apollo did)

Kennedy Space Center LC-39B, 1 April 2026, 22:35 UTC. Artemis II — first crewed lunar mission since Apollo 17 (1972). Crew: Reid Wiseman (NASA, cmdr), Victor Glover (NASA), Christina Koch (NASA, first woman on a lunar mission), Jeremy Hansen (CSA, first non-American to fly to the Moon).
Orion + ICPS finished post-launch checkout in high Earth orbit. The crew flew Orion around the spent ICPS for the manual proximity-operations demo unique to this mission.

Orion's own service-module (ESM) main engine fired about 25 hours after launch, on flight day 2 (the ICPS had only raised the perigee), placing Orion + crew on a five-day free-return path to the Moon. The trajectory is designed so the Moon's gravity bends Orion straight back to Earth even if the engine fails — no LOI burn needed.
Refines the free-return trajectory toward the Moon.

6 April 2026: closest approach ~6,545 km (4,067 mi) above the lunar far side, and 406,771 km from Earth — farther than any humans had travelled, beating Apollo 13's 1970 record. No lunar orbit: Artemis II was a flyby test of Orion's life support and comms over a 9-day deep-space flight, ahead of the first landing, now planned for Artemis IV.
Targets the Pacific splashdown ellipse off San Diego.

10 April 2026 (11 April UTC). Orion re-entered at about 11 km/s (lunar return velocity) on a shorter entry path than Artemis I's skip entry — chosen after Artemis I's heat-shield char loss — and splashed down in the Pacific off San Diego. First crewed deep-space mission of the 21st century.
First crewed flight beyond low-Earth orbit since Apollo 17 (1972) — and the mission that inspired this project

The Artemis program's first crewed flight, and the spark that became Orrery. On 1 April 2026 NASA's SLS Block 1 launched an Orion spacecraft with four astronauts — Reid Wiseman (CDR), Victor Glover (PLT), Christina Koch (MS), and CSA's Jeremy Hansen (MS) — onto a free-return trajectory that swung them around the Moon's far side about 6,500 km above the surface and brought them home without any lunar-orbit insertion burn. At 406,771 km from Earth they travelled farther than any humans before them, beating Apollo 13's 1970 record. After a 9-day flight Orion splashed down in the Pacific off San Diego on 10 April. The flight qualified Orion's life support, navigation and heat shield for crewed missions ahead of the first landing, now planned for Artemis IV.
Orion lifts off from KSC LC-39B with four crew aboard.
Trans-lunar injection burn by Orion's service-module engine on flight day 2 — Orion leaves Earth orbit for a cislunar trajectory.
Closest approach over the far side, ~6,500 km altitude, and the farthest humans have travelled: 406,771 km from Earth. No orbit insertion — free-return geometry slings Orion back to Earth.
Orion re-entry and Pacific Ocean splashdown.
